beats.text: Try to tickle yourself. Nothing, right?
Your brain predicts the touch before it happens. And what's predicted feels weaker.
Researchers built a robot that stroked people's palm, controlled by their own other hand.
When the robot added a tiny delay, just a fraction of a second, it started to tickle.
Your brain cancels out its own surprises.
That's why you can't tickle yourself. And why someone else's touch always feels stronger.

sources: Blakemore, Frith & Wolpert (1999). Spatio-temporal prediction modulates the perception of self-produced stimuli. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience 11(5). Robot interface; ticklishness rose with delays of 100-300 ms and with rotation.
Shergill et al. (2003). Two eyes for an eye: the neuroscience of force escalation. Science 301: self-generated forces feel weaker. Via BPS/PsyBlog summaries.
